items.quote: Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings.
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish the letter’s sender, Claudius Lysias, from its recipient, Governor Felix.
items.reason: Felix is a plausible mistake because his name appears in the heading, but “To” marks him as the recipient; Claudius Lysias is the sender.

items.quote: Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish the stated reason for Uzziah’s eagerness from the priests’ separate act of hurrying him out.
items.reason: The priests’ action is a nearby possible cause of his departure, but the passage explicitly attributes his eagerness to the Lord’s affliction.

items.quote: When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him. As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him
items.contrast: The reader must resolve whether the departure and subsequent death concern the man of God or the prophet who had brought him back.
items.reason: The nearby prophet makes the pronouns initially ambiguous, but he prepares the donkey for the man of God, who then goes on his way; the old prophet remains associated with the city where the death is reported.

items.quote: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David’s rescue; he struck the Philistine down and killed him.
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish Ishbi-Benob, the attacker Abishai kills, from David, the person Abishai rescues.
items.reason: David is a nearby possible referent for “him,” but the sentence says David is rescued and that “the Philistine” is struck down. In context, that Philistine is Ishbi-Benob.

items.quote: Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the time of the captivity of the land.
items.contrast: The reader must attach the captivity deadline to the priests’ service rather than attach the Shiloh timeline for using the idol to that service.
items.reason: The Shiloh period is a plausible mistake because it follows immediately, but it describes how long the idol was used. The priesthood is explicitly said to last until the captivity of the land.
